title: Semi-Supervised Learning for Molecular Graphs via Ensemble Consensus
topic: General Machine Learning->Unsupervised and Semi-supervised Learning
claim: Training members against their own ensemble's consensus on unlabeled data forms a self-reinforcing loop that drives models toward flatter minima.
layout: 2 panels: left loop diagram flowing clockwise, right line plot with colorbar
description: The left panel is a schematic of the semi-supervised loop. A labeled-data icon (a small water molecule) sends a thick red arrow labeled 'Supervised Loss' into a tall rounded box listing ensemble members f_θ1 through f_θM. An unlabeled-data icon (a larger molecule) sends a blue arrow down to an 'Ensemble Prediction' box. Red and blue arrows run from the member box to the prediction box. A blue 'Consensus Loss' arrow curves back from the prediction box to the members, and the bold words 'SSL Loop' sit in the centre of the cycle. The right panel is a line plot of the trace of the Hessian of the loss against training epochs, from 0 to 1000. Its curves are coloured by coupling weight, from yellow at 0 to dark purple at 1, and the dark purple curves end up lowest, which shows flatter minima.
caption: (Left) Schematic of the semi-supervised ensemble training loop. Individual ensemble members fθ are trained on labeled data via a standard supervised loss. Simultaneously, the full ensemble’s aggregated prediction on unlabeled data acts as a target for a consensus loss. Since the ensemble aggregate typically outperforms individual members, this creates a self-reinforcing loop where the collective prediction guides individual improvement. (Right) Training with ensemble consensus (provably) makes the model converge to more flat points in the loss landscape. This is shown here on the dataset QM9 target ZPVE as measured here by the trace of the Hessian of the loss on validation data.
abstract: Machine learning is transforming molecular sciences by accelerating property prediction, simulation, and the discovery of new molecules and materials. Acquiring labeled data in these domains is often costly and time-consuming, whereas large collections of unlabeled molecular data are readily available. Standard semi-supervised learning methods often rely on label-preserving augmentations, which are challenging to design in the molecular domain, where minor changes can drastically alter properties. In this work, we show that semi-supervised methods that rely on an ensemble consensus can boost predictive accuracy across a diverse range of molecular datasets, task types, and graph neural network architectures. We find that training with an ensemble consensus objective increases robustness in models and exhibits an effect similar to knowledge distillation; an individual member of an ensemble trained this way outperforms a full ensemble trained in a traditional supervised fashion in almost all cases. In addition, this type of semi-supervised training reduces calibration error.
